title: Stranded: I've Come From a Plane That Crashed on the Mountains
full_review:
On Oct. 13, 1972, a plane carrying a team of rugby players from a Catholic school in Montevideo, Uruguay, to a match in Chile crashed in a remote section of the Andes Mountains.

More than 10 weeks later, two of the 16 remaining survivors, having hiked 44 miles over peaks 13,000 feet high, finally made contact with their first outsider, a Chilean shepherd, and were soon guiding a squad of helicopters to rescue their friends.

Among the accounts of what these students, all from privileged backgrounds, endured in the interval are Piers Paul Read's 1974 book, "Alive: The Story of the Andes Survivors," and its 1993 screen adaptation by director Frank Marshall, called simply "Alive."

In "Stranded: I've Come From a Plane That Crashed on the Mountains" (Zeitgeist), documentarian Gonzalo Arijon, a childhood friend of several of the athletes, provides first-hand descriptions of their ordeal. Using interviews with the now middle-age men, some of them filmed on a recent visit to the crash site, as well as archival footage and silent, haunting reenactments, he evokes their desperate heroism and their profound, indispensable spirit of unity.

The film also explores the religious implications of their experience as one survivor describes a crisis of faith that was resolved by joining his companions in the recitation of the rosary, while another speaks of his feelings of closeness to -- and total dependence on -- God.

As news coverage of their return reveals, a disturbing question quickly arose amid the euphoria: How had the young men held out for so long with no available food source? The unsettling answer was that, faced with seemingly certain starvation, they had resorted to cannibalism.

While this disclosure, exploited by the press, stirred considerable controversy, the survivors are unanimous in defending the morality of their decision. Their moving gratitude for the gift of continued life and the readiness more than one expressed to have his own body sustain the others after death bring to mind the self-giving of Christ in the Eucharist.

And, in fact, drawing on an analogy offered at the time by the charismatic student they regarded as their leader who died before being rescued, several compare the orderly yet harrowing procedure they followed to receiving holy Communion. While not explicitly accepting this analysis, then-Coadjutor Archbishop Carlos Parteli Keller and then-Auxiliary Bishop Andres Maria Rubio Garcia of Montevideo, Uruguay, both endorsed the extreme measure as morally justified.

In Spanish. Subtitles.

The film contains mature themes, one use of the F-word and a few crass expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
